items.title: A Talk on Learning Languages
items.tvi: Bài nói về học ngoại ngữ
items.text: When people ask me how I learned five languages, they usually expect me to reveal some kind of secret method. The truth is rather less exciting. The most important thing I did was to make the language part of my daily routine, even for just twenty minutes, rather than studying for four hours once a week. Little and often beats long and rare, because the brain needs repeated contact to remember. The second thing was to stop being afraid of mistakes. For years I barely spoke Spanish, because I was waiting until I could speak it perfectly. It was only when I moved to Mexico and had no choice that I really improved. And finally, I chose materials I actually enjoyed: films, podcasts about football, cookery programmes. If you're bored, you'll give up, no matter how good the textbook is. items.title: An Architect on Designing Homes
items.tvi: Kiến trúc sư bàn về thiết kế nhà
lines: You've said that most new apartments are designed for people who don't exist. What do you mean by that?

Developers tend to design for an imaginary average family: two parents, two children, both adults working nine to five. But that family is becoming the exception. We have elderly people living alone, adult children living with parents well into their thirties, people working from home. The standard layout simply doesn't fit.
So what would you do differently?

Flexibility, above all. Walls that can be moved without major building work, rooms that can be divided or combined as needs change. In one project, we designed apartments where a small studio could be separated from the main flat with its own entrance, so a grandparent could live independently but close by.
Isn't that more expensive to build?

Initially, slightly. But if you consider that people won't need to move every time their life changes, it's far more economical over the lifetime of the building. The real obstacle isn't cost, it's habit. Developers know what sells, and they're reluctant to take risks.
Are you optimistic that this will change?
Cautiously. Buyers are becoming more demanding, and once a few developers prove the model works, others usually follow.

items.title: A Lecture on Misinformation
items.tvi: Bài giảng về tin sai lệch
items.text: One of the most counterintuitive findings in research on misinformation is that correcting a false claim can sometimes make people remember it more strongly. If a news story repeats a myth in order to debunk it, some readers later recall the myth but forget that it was false. Repetition, it seems, breeds familiarity, and familiarity is easily mistaken for truth. This doesn't mean we should stop correcting falsehoods; on balance, corrections do reduce belief in misinformation. But it does suggest that how we correct matters enormously. Researchers now recommend leading with the facts rather than the myth, mentioning the false claim only once, and explaining why it is wrong, not merely that it is wrong. People find it difficult to abandon an explanation unless they are offered a better one to replace it. Another promising approach is so-called prebunking: warning people in advance about the techniques used to mislead them, such as emotional language or fake experts. Rather like a vaccine, this seems to give people a degree of resistance before they encounter the misinformation itself.

items.title: A Radio Piece on Urban Heat
items.tvi: Phóng sự về nhiệt đô thị
items.text: On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees hotter than the countryside just a few kilometres away. This is known as the urban heat island effect, and it's caused by the materials cities are built from. Concrete, asphalt and dark rooftops absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, so temperatures never fall as much as they should. Air conditioners make the problem worse, pumping hot air into the streets to keep buildings cool. The consequences are far from trivial. Heat waves are now one of the deadliest forms of extreme weather, particularly for elderly people and outdoor workers. Fortunately, the solutions are relatively well understood. Planting trees can reduce street temperatures significantly, while painting roofs white reflects sunlight rather than absorbing it. Some cities are going further, building so-called green corridors, linked parks and waterways that allow cooler air to flow through dense neighbourhoods. The challenge is less technical than financial: such measures require long-term investment, and their benefits, while substantial, are spread across many years.

items.title: Interview with a Translator
lines: You've translated more than thirty novels from Vietnamese into English. What's the hardest part?

Without doubt, forms of address. Vietnamese uses kinship terms constantly: anh, chị, em, cô, chú. Each one tells you about age, relationship, even emotional distance. English has just 'you'. A whole layer of meaning disappears unless you find other ways to express it.
How do you deal with that?

items.title: A Talk on Decision Fatigue
items.tvi: Bài nói về mệt mỏi khi ra quyết định
items.text: Have you ever noticed that you make worse choices at the end of a long day? Psychologists call this decision fatigue: the idea that our capacity to make careful decisions gets used up, rather like a muscle that tires with use. One frequently quoted study of judges found that they were far more likely to grant prisoners parole early in the morning and just after lunch, and far less likely to do so just before a break. When tired, the researchers suggested, people tend to fall back on the default option, which for a judge is to say no. I should add that this study has been criticised, and some of its findings may have other explanations. But the general idea fits many people's experience, and it has practical implications. Some successful people deliberately reduce trivial decisions, wearing similar clothes every day or eating the same breakfast, so that they have more energy for decisions that matter. You don't need to go that far, but it may be worth scheduling important choices for the morning, and being a little suspicious of anything you decide at eleven o'clock at night.

qs.a: Tired judges tended to choose the safer default

items.title: A Museum Curator's Talk
items.tvi: Bài nói của người phụ trách bảo tàng
items.text: When visitors come to this exhibition, they often ask why some of the objects look so ordinary: a broken bowl, a child's sandal, a handful of coins. They expect a museum to be full of treasures. But for archaeologists, everyday objects are often far more revealing than gold. A king's crown tells us about one person; a cooking pot tells us about thousands. From the residue left inside these pots, for instance, we've been able to work out what people ate, which crops they grew and even how trade routes connected this coast to China and India. The sandal you see in the third case belonged to a child of perhaps six or seven. We know that because of its size, but also because it was repaired three times, suggesting the family couldn't afford a new one. Small details like that bring the past to life in a way that treasure rarely does. So as you walk around today, I'd encourage you to spend as much time with the humble objects as with the spectacular ones.

qs.a: They reveal how ordinary people lived

items.title: A Report on Food Waste
items.tvi: Phóng sự về lãng phí thực phẩm
items.text: Roughly a third of all food produced worldwide is never eaten. In poorer countries, most of this loss happens early in the supply chain, through inadequate storage, transport and refrigeration. In wealthier countries, by contrast, the largest share is thrown away by shops and households. Supermarkets reject fruit and vegetables that are the wrong shape or size, and consumers routinely discard food that is perfectly safe simply because it has passed a 'best before' date. Many people confuse this with a 'use by' date, which genuinely relates to safety. 'Best before' is merely about quality: a biscuit may be slightly less crisp, but it's not going to make you ill. Some countries are now taking action. France has made it illegal for large supermarkets to throw away unsold food that is still edible; it must instead be donated to charities. Elsewhere, apps connect restaurants with customers who can buy leftover meals cheaply at the end of the day. Such measures help, but campaigners argue that real change will require a shift in attitudes, so that we see food not as something disposable but as something that took resources, energy and labour to produce.

What is the difference between 'best before' and 'use by'?
qs.a: 'Best before' is about quality, 'use by' about safety

w: Shops must sell food more cheaply

items.title: A Philosopher on Luck
items.tvi: Nhà triết học bàn về may mắn
items.text: We tend to judge people by what they do, but a moment's reflection reveals how much of what they do is shaped by circumstances beyond their control. Philosophers call this moral luck. Consider two drivers who, after a party, each drive home having had a glass too many. One arrives safely; the other, through no greater fault of his own, encounters a child who has run into the road. The second driver will be prosecuted and condemned; the first will, at most, feel a twinge of guilt the next morning. Yet their choices were identical. What differed was luck. The unsettling implication is that our judgements of praise and blame are, to a considerable degree, judgements of outcome rather than intention. One might respond that we should therefore judge only intentions. But that position has its own difficulties: it would require us to treat the careless driver who kills a child exactly as we treat the careless driver who gets home safely, and very few people find that intuitively acceptable. The problem, in other words, is not easily resolved. Perhaps the most we can do is to remain aware of it, and to temper our condemnation of others with the recognition that, but for circumstance, we might have stood where they stand.

qs.a: Identical choices can be judged differently because of outcomes

One driver was more careful than the other

qs.a: Most people would find the result hard to accept

items.title: Two Critics Debate a Novel
items.tvi: Hai nhà phê bình tranh luận về một cuốn tiểu thuyết
lines: I'll be blunt: I found the novel insufferably self-indulgent. Six hundred pages, and the plot could be summarised on a postcard.
But surely plot isn't the point. It's a novel about consciousness, about the texture of a single day. Complaining that nothing happens is rather like complaining that a symphony has no dialogue.
That's a seductive comparison, but a symphony doesn't ask for twenty hours of my time. At some point the reader is entitled to ask what all this attentiveness is in service of.
I'd argue it's in service of attentiveness itself. We spend our lives skimming. A book that forces us to slow down and notice is doing something genuinely countercultural.
Countercultural, perhaps. Enjoyable, rarely. I kept feeling that the author was more interested in demonstrating his sensitivity than in sharing it.
Now that's a fairer criticism, and I'll concede there are passages that tip into showing off. But the final chapter, the mother at the window, redeemed all of it for me.
I'll grant you the final chapter. I just wish I hadn't had to wade through five hundred pages to reach it.

items.title: A Talk on the History of Timekeeping
items.tvi: Bài nói về lịch sử đo thời gian
items.text: It's easy to assume that people have always lived by the clock, but standardised time is a remarkably recent invention. Until the mid-nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time, set by the position of the sun. When it was noon in one city, it might be several minutes earlier or later in another just a short distance away. For most purposes this hardly mattered. What changed everything was the railway. Trains travelling between towns with different local times made timetables a nightmare, and collisions a genuine danger. British railway companies began adopting a single standard time in the 1840s, and by the 1880s the idea of dividing the world into time zones had been agreed internationally. Not everyone welcomed it. Some local communities resented what they saw as an imposition by distant authorities, and a few clocks were deliberately kept showing both local and railway time. Historians have argued that standard time did more than coordinate trains: it changed how people experienced their days, subordinating the natural rhythm of sunrise and sunset to the requirements of industry and commerce.

qs.a: By the position of the sun

qs.a: Different local times caused confusion and danger

qs.a: People's days became organised around industry, not nature

items.title: Interview with an Economist
lines: Your new book argues that economic growth, as conventionally measured, tells us surprisingly little about wellbeing. Isn't that a rather fashionable position?

It's become fashionable, which is not the same as being wrong. GDP measures the value of goods and services exchanged in the market. It counts the money spent cleaning up after a disaster as a positive contribution, while ignoring entirely the unpaid work of caring for children or elderly relatives. It was never designed to measure how well people's lives are going, and its inventor said so explicitly.
But growth has lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Surely that matters?

Enormously, and I'd never dismiss it. Below a certain level of income, growth and wellbeing move very closely together. My argument concerns richer societies, where the relationship weakens considerably. Beyond that point, things like health, security, the quality of relationships and a sense of purpose seem to matter at least as much as additional income.
So what would you have governments do, abandon GDP?

Not abandon it, supplement it. Several countries now publish wellbeing dashboards alongside conventional figures. The danger isn't that we measure growth; it's that we treat it as the only thing worth measuring.

When does the economist say growth and wellbeing are closely linked?

items.title: A Lecture on Memory and Testimony
items.tvi: Bài giảng về trí nhớ và lời khai
items.text: Courts have long placed great weight on eyewitness testimony, and juries in particular find a confident witness extraordinarily persuasive. Yet decades of research have shown that memory is not a recording but a reconstruction, assembled anew each time we recall an event and vulnerable to influence at every stage. In a classic series of experiments, participants who watched film of a car accident were later asked how fast the cars were going when they either 'hit' or 'smashed into' each other. Those who heard the word 'smashed' gave higher estimates of speed and, a week later, were more than twice as likely to report having seen broken glass, although there was none. Equally troubling is the relationship between confidence and accuracy. A witness's confidence often grows over time, especially if they receive feedback suggesting they identified the right person, while the accuracy of their memory does not. By the time of the trial, a witness who was initially hesitant may testify with complete certainty. None of this implies that witnesses are dishonest. The point is that sincerity and reliability are different things, and a justice system that conflates them is likely, sooner or later, to convict the innocent.

qs.a: As something rebuilt each time we remember

qs.a: An honest witness is not necessarily an accurate one

items.title: Colleagues Discuss Artificial Intelligence at Work
items.tvi: Đồng nghiệp bàn về trí tuệ nhân tạo trong công việc
lines: Have you tried the new drafting tool the firm's introduced? It produced a perfectly respectable contract in about thirty seconds.

I have, and that's precisely what worries me. Not that it's bad, but that it's good enough. Junior lawyers have always learned by drafting precisely these kinds of documents. If the machine does it, how do they ever develop judgement?
I suppose they'd learn by reviewing the machine's work instead.

Perhaps, but reviewing isn't the same as creating. You only really understand why a clause is worded a particular way when you've tried and failed to word it yourself. I worry we'll end up with a generation of lawyers who can spot that something looks plausible without understanding why it might be wrong.
That's a fair concern, though people said much the same about calculators and maths.

They did, and to some extent they were right. Mental arithmetic did decline. The question is whether what we lose matters. With calculators, arguably not much. With legal judgement, I'm far less sure.
So you'd rather we didn't use it?
No, I'd rather we used it deliberately, and kept some tasks for people precisely because they're how expertise is formed.

items.title: A Talk on Translation and Culture
items.tvi: Bài nói về dịch thuật và văn hoá
items.text: It is sometimes claimed that certain words are untranslatable: that the Portuguese 'saudade', for example, or the Vietnamese 'thương', capture emotions for which other languages simply have no equivalent. The claim is appealing, and it flatters the cultures concerned, but it needs careful handling. Of course no single English word corresponds exactly to 'thương', which can encompass love, pity, tenderness and a kind of protective concern. But the absence of a single word is not the same as the absence of the concept. English speakers are perfectly capable of experiencing, and describing, that cluster of feelings; they merely require a phrase rather than a word. What the existence of such terms does reveal is which experiences a culture has found important enough to lexicalise, to package into a single convenient unit. That is genuinely interesting, but it tells us about emphasis and attention rather than about the limits of human feeling. To insist otherwise is to slip towards the view that speakers of different languages inhabit sealed worlds, a view that the everyday success of translators, however imperfect, rather contradicts.

qs.a: The idea is attractive but often exaggerated

items.title: A Debate on Tourism
lines: The figures speak for themselves. Tourism provides millions of jobs and has transformed entire regions. To talk about restricting it is a luxury only the comfortable can afford.

Nobody's disputing the economic benefits. But you're treating tourism as a single thing, when its effects depend entirely on how it's managed. Look at towns where cruise ships unload thousands of visitors for four hours. They spend almost nothing locally, crowd out residents and leave behind rubbish and rising rents.
Those are problems of management, not of tourism itself.

Exactly my point. Which is why limits, sensibly applied, aren't anti-tourism. A cap on daily visitors, a tax that funds local services, rules on short-term rentals. These protect the very qualities that attract people in the first place.
And who decides where the cap should be? It's very easy for a city council to price out ordinary travellers while the wealthy carry on as before.
That's a legitimate risk, and I'd want any scheme designed with that in mind. But the alternative, doing nothing, has its own victims, and they're usually the people who live there.

items.title: A Scientist on Uncertainty
items.tvi: Nhà khoa học bàn về sự không chắc chắn
items.text: One of the most persistent misunderstandings between scientists and the public concerns the word 'theory'. In everyday speech, a theory is a guess, a hunch that may or may not be correct. In science, it means something closer to the opposite: a well-substantiated explanation that has survived repeated attempts to disprove it. When a scientist says that evolution is 'only a theory', she is not expressing doubt; she is placing it in the same category as the theory of gravity. Similar confusion surrounds uncertainty. Scientists are trained to state the limits of their knowledge, to attach margins of error to their estimates and to acknowledge alternative explanations. Within science, this is a mark of rigour. Outside it, it is frequently heard as weakness or evasion, and it can be exploited by those who wish to cast doubt on inconvenient findings. The solution is not for scientists to abandon caution, which would undermine the very thing that makes their conclusions trustworthy. It is rather to explain, patiently and repeatedly, that uncertainty about details is entirely compatible with confidence about the larger picture.

w: A guess that is probably wrong

What does the speaker recommend scientists do?

items.title: Friends Discuss Ambition
items.tvi: Bạn bè bàn về tham vọng
lines: Do you ever feel you've settled? I look at people from university running companies and writing books, and I'm still in the same job I had ten years ago.
Actually, yes, most days. That's what makes it so confusing. I feel as though I ought to want more.
Ought according to whom, though? It sounds as if you're measuring yourself against a story about success that you've never actually chosen.
Maybe. But isn't a bit of ambition healthy? Otherwise we'd all just stagnate.

Of course, but ambition for what? There's a difference between wanting to get better at something you care about and wanting to look successful to people you barely know. The first tends to make people happier; the second rarely does, because there's always someone further ahead.
So you think I should stop comparing myself?
I think you should notice when you're doing it, and ask whether the comparison tells you anything you actually want to know.
